title: Check resource identity before closing a reused fd or recursively deleting a replaced root
applies_when: A leak hypothesis proposes unconditional cleanup after a filesystem root is rebound or a fork callback may replace a file descriptor. Inspect the complete ownership and identity checks, not just the skipped close or rollback branch.
lesson: A pathname or fd number can designate a different resource by cleanup time. OpenClaw deliberately skips ordinary rollback and stage deletion after INSTALL_BASE_CHANGED; inspect the retained root identity and test an outside sentinel after a real root rebind. Filelock's complete before-fork callback first retries unverified descriptor identities; child cleanup closes only a matching device/inode. Persistent identity failure is a different case: an earlier child callback can reuse the fd for an unrelated file, so unconditional close can damage that replacement. Pair normal owned cleanup and recovered-identity closure with a real same-number fd replacement or root rebind. Seven selected upstream Linux fork cases passed, including registration/rollback failure and replacement-fd preservation. This refutes the truncated-callback explanation, not every possible leak.
avoid_when: Retained resources can still have operational costs, and identity checks alone do not eliminate races. Do not use this counterexample to waive prompt cleanup of known-owned failed acquisitions, late worker arrivals or successful ownership handoffs. Filelock evidence is seven selected Linux CPython fork cases with task-only generated version metadata, not full backend/platform or packaging qualification. OpenClaw evidence is source/test inspection only, not executed installation tests. Safe identity-bound cleanup may be possible; demonstrate its ownership contract rather than inferring authority from the old name or number.

evidence.note: The stable-root check compares real paths; the ordinary temp cleanup recursively removes a pathname. Its existence does not authorize removal after replacement. Source inspection.
Ordinary mutation/removal is bound to the retained owner and root/directory identities. Source inspection.
The changed-root failure warns and skips the ordinary rollback/stage-deletion branch. Source inspection, not a generic missing-finally defect.
The rebound-root fixture requires an untouched outside target and a warning, unlike ordinary cleanup controls. These TypeScript tests were inspected, not run.
The before-fork callback invokes _verify_unverified_descriptors; child detachment skips unknown or nonmatching identities instead of closing by fd number alone.

Native Linux selected upstream tests passed: recovering fstat after registration/rollback failure permits child closure, while persistent identity failure plus an earlier child callback preserves a different file reusing the same fd. Failure injection covers these cases, not all lock behavior.
